name: Red Lake agreement under the Nelson Act, signed July 8, 1889 (cession of the Red Lake Reservation outside the diminished reserve)
aka: Nelson Act agreement with the Red Lake Chippewa
citation: Act of January 14, 1889, ch. 24, 25 Stat. 642; agreement printed in H. R. Ex. Doc. 247, 51st Cong., 1st sess.
nations: Red Lake Band of Chippewa Indians (Miskwaagamiiwi-Zaaga'iganiwi Anishinaabeg)
the other Chippewa (Ojibwe) of Minnesota, whose assent the Act required for the Red Lake cession
promises: Section 1: the Red Lake cession was valid only if assented to in writing by two-thirds of the male adults of all the Chippewa in Minnesota and approved by the President; Indians already holding allotments were not to be disturbed without their own consent.
Section 3: the Red Lake Indians were to be allotted land in severalty on the Red Lake Reservation, not removed to White Earth.

Sections 4 to 6: ceded pine lands to be examined, appraised at no less than $3 per thousand feet of pine and sold at public auction in 40-acre parcels for no less than the appraised value; other ceded land sold only to actual settlers under the homestead law at $1.25 an acre.

Section 7: net proceeds held in the Treasury as a permanent fund for all the Chippewa in Minnesota at 5 percent interest for fifty years, half the interest paid to heads of families, a quarter per capita and a quarter for schools, with the fund then divided in equal shares; the United States to advance $90,000 a year as interest until the fund reached $3,000,000.

breaches.what: The Red Lake Band claimed an accounting for all lands and timber in Royce area 706 and the difference between their fair value and what the United States credited to the Band for them. The Commission let that claim go forward in 1972, and in 1976 sent it, with the Band's related Docket 189-A and the Minnesota Chippewa Tribe's Docket 19, to the Court of Claims undecided.

breaches.what: Red Lake Nation leaders say the United States used fraud and deception in negotiating the 1889 agreement, and that the government's map after the talks split Upper Red Lake rather than following the outline the chiefs had drawn, which the chiefs called false at the time.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Red Lake Tribal Chairman Darrell Seki Sr. and Tribal Secretary Sam Strong, as reported by the Bemidji Pioneer

breaches.quote: fraud and deception on the part of the United States in negotiating the 1889 agreement with the Red Lake chiefs

landTaken: Royce describes the cession as all of the Red Lake Reservation outside the boundaries the agreement drew around the upper and lower Red Lakes (area 706); he gives no acreage.
compensation: Under the Act, payment was the sale proceeds placed in a permanent fund for all the Chippewa in Minnesota (Section 7), not a price paid to the Band. No payment specific to the Red Lake Band was traced.
today: The claim that the 1889 cession was a taking without consent failed: the Commission held in 1972 that it was bound by the Court of Claims' finding in Chippewa Indians v. United States, 80 Ct. Cl. 410 (1935), that the Chippewa of Minnesota, Red Lake included, gave the consent the Act required, and that Band counsel had admitted that assent. Red Lake Nation leaders said in 2023 they were seeking the restoration of the east part of Upper Red Lake.

nationVoice.summary: Tribal Chairman Darrell Seki Sr. says the United States used fraud and deception in negotiating the 1889 agreement, that the government map produced afterwards split Upper Red Lake instead of following the outline the chiefs drew, and that the chiefs rejected that map at the time; Tribal Secretary Sam Strong calls the loss of the lake a theft.

nationVoice.nation: Red Lake Nation (Red Lake Band of Chippewa Indians)
nationVoice.summary: The Nation says the United States broke treaty promises on July 8, 1889, that its reservation of 3,260,000 acres was forced to cede 2,905,000 acres as surplus, leaving a little more than 300,000 acres, that the Band successfully resisted allotment, and that in 1904 officials returned and forced it to cede more of the land set aside in 1889.

openQuestions: The agreement itself (H. R. Ex. Doc. 247, 51st Cong., 1st sess.) was not opened; its terms here are the Nelson Act's, which the agreement accepted, and Royce's description.

Docket 189 (Red Lake Band, 1973) concerns pre-1889 survey errors that excluded Tracts A and C from the reservation; it is not a finding on this agreement and is left out. The outcome of the Red Lake accounting claims (Dockets 189-A and 189-B) after their 1976 transfer to the Court of Claims was not found.
The Red Lake Nation's own website was not opened; its account here comes from leaders quoted in a newspaper.

treaties.json lists Rocky Boy's, Turtle Mountain and White Earth as present-day tribes for this entry but not the Red Lake Band by its own name first; Royce names the Red Lake Chippewa as the band that signed on July 8, 1889, with the Pembina signing on July 29, 1889.
treaties.json gives this entry and cession-1889-07-08-chippewa-red-lake-and-pembina-bands the same date and transaction; Royce shows the ceded part as 706 and the diminished reservation as 707.

plain.promised: Under the Nelson Act the Red Lake Chippewa gave up most of their reservation. The land was to be sold at set minimum prices, with the money held in a fund paying interest to all the Chippewa in Minnesota for fifty years.
plain.happened: No finding of a breach was found. A taking claim failed on a 1935 court finding that the required consent was given. The Band's claim over land and timber sales went to the Court of Claims in 1976; its outcome was not found.
plain.today: Red Lake Nation leaders say the 1889 agreement was obtained by fraud and deception and are seeking the return of the east part of Upper Red Lake.
